title: Graceful Degradation & Load Shedding
summary: Doing less instead of doing nothing — fallback responses, shedding low-priority traffic, and stopping a cascade before it spreads to callers.

slides.markdown:
When part of a system is overloaded or failing, the default outcome is a hard error for everyone. A better system **degrades gracefully**: it does less — fewer features, staler data, lower quality — rather than nothing at all, and it sheds low-priority work early to protect the core path.

This topic covers fallback responses, load shedding, deciding what to shed first, and cascading failure — the mechanism by which one overloaded service's problem becomes every one of its callers' problem too if none of this is in place.

slides.sectionTitle: Graceful degradation: doing less instead of doing nothing
slides.markdown:
**Graceful degradation** means a system under stress keeps its core function working by giving up something less essential, rather than failing the whole request. A product page that can't reach the reviews service should still show the product and price — not a blank error page — just without reviews for now.

This requires deciding *in advance* which parts of a response are essential and which are enhancements, so the system knows what it's allowed to drop under pressure. Retrofitting this decision during an actual incident is too late — it needs to be designed into the response structure ahead of time.

The test for a well-degraded system: when a non-critical dependency fails, most users don't notice, they just get slightly less.

slides.sectionTitle: Fallback responses: cached/stale/default data instead of an error
slides.markdown:
The concrete mechanism behind graceful degradation is a **fallback**: when the real call fails or times out, serve something else instead of propagating the error. Common fallbacks, roughly in order of quality: a **cached** response from moments ago (fresh enough that users won't notice), a **stale** cache entry kept around specifically for this purpose (older, but still meaningful — yesterday's recommendation list beats none), or a **static default** (a generic "popular items" list when personalization is unavailable).

The fallback tier you can offer depends on what you've deliberately kept around for this purpose — a stale-data fallback only works if something cached the data before the outage, which means planning for it ahead of time, not improvising it mid-incident.

Always attach the fallback decision to a circuit breaker or timeout, not to every individual error — reacting to the *pattern* of failure, not one flaky response, avoids flip-flopping into fallback mode unnecessarily.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a feature falling back to a degraded mode under load
slides.markdown:
![Product page falling back to a static list when Recommendations fails](assets/graceful-degradation.svg)

The page's core purpose — letting someone see and buy the product — survives untouched in both paths. Only the enhancement (personalized recommendations) is what gets swapped for something cheaper and more resilient.

Notice the fallback path skips calling Recommendations entirely rather than waiting on it and timing out — that avoids tying up a request thread on a call that's already known to be unhealthy.

slides.sectionTitle: Load shedding: dropping low-priority requests to protect the core path
slides.markdown:
**Load shedding** is the more drastic sibling of graceful degradation: instead of serving a lesser version of a request, the system rejects some requests outright — usually with a fast, cheap `503` — so it has enough capacity left to properly serve the ones it keeps.

The logic is counterintuitive at first: deliberately refusing some traffic *improves* overall outcomes, because a system past its capacity serving everyone badly (timeouts, queued requests, cascading retries) delivers worse aggregate results than a system serving 80% of requests well and shedding the rest immediately.

Shedding decisions should happen as early and cheaply as possible — checking a load signal and returning a fast rejection is far cheaper than accepting the request and failing deep into the call chain after real work has already been spent on it.

slides.sectionTitle: Prioritizing traffic: what to shed first
slides.markdown:
Shedding needs a priority order, decided ahead of the incident, not improvised during it. A common scheme: **critical** (checkout, login — never shed if avoidable), **standard** (browsing, search — shed under sustained pressure), **best-effort** (analytics pings, background sync, prefetching — shed first, always safe to drop).

The priority signal has to travel with the request — a header or field set at the edge — so any service deep in the call chain can make a consistent shedding decision without needing to know the caller's full context.

Getting this wrong in the obvious way — shedding indiscriminately by arrival order — means checkout requests get dropped exactly as often as background analytics pings, which defeats the entire point of having a priority scheme at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: shedding at the edge vs deep in the call chain
slides.markdown:
| | Shedding at the edge (gateway/LB) | Shedding deep in the call chain |
|---|---|---|
| Cost of a shed request | Cheap — rejected before any real work happens | Expensive — upstream work already spent before the drop |
| Visibility into true bottleneck | Limited — the edge doesn't know which internal service is actually saturated | Accurate — shed right where the real capacity limit is |
| Best for | Coarse, cheap protection against overall overload | Precise protection for one specific saturated dependency |

**How to decide:** shed at the edge for blunt, cheap protection against a general overload, and add deep shedding at a specific service only when that service, not the whole system, is the actual bottleneck — the two aren't mutually exclusive.

slides.sectionTitle: Cascading failure: how one overloaded service takes down its callers
slides.markdown:
**Cascading failure** is what happens when neither degradation nor shedding is in place: Service B gets overloaded and starts responding slowly. Service A, calling B without a fallback or timeout budget, has its own threads tied up waiting on B — so A becomes slow too. A's callers now experience the same thing, and the slowdown propagates outward, one hop at a time, until services that never directly touched B are failing because of it.

Each individual hop's behavior looks locally reasonable ("just wait for the response"), but the aggregate effect is a slowdown that spreads far beyond the original bottleneck.

Every mechanism in this group — timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks, shedding — exists to break one link in this propagation chain; that's why they're usually deployed together rather than any single one alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: no fallback path, so any failure becomes a hard user-facing error
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If a non-critical dependency fails, it's fine — that one feature just errors out."

**Why it's wrong:** without a designed fallback, "that feature errors out" often means the whole page or request fails, because the response-building code has no path that produces a partial result — one failed call throws, and the exception takes the entire response down with it, not just the recommendations widget.

**Correct model:** design response construction so a non-critical section's failure is caught locally and replaced with a fallback (cached data, a static default, or simply omitting that section) — the request as a whole should only fail when something genuinely essential fails, not whenever any single dependency has a bad moment.
